title: The Way You Speak to Yourself Matters
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece treats a leader's internal narration as a performance variable rather than a private quirk. The author accepts that constant inner commentary is natural and stress-relieving, then argues that its quality is what determines whether it helps or harms. The causal claim is directional: poor thoughts drive poor performance more than the reverse, and habitual self-trash-talk makes the confidence required for good work nearly impossible to summon. Rather than prescribing vague positivity, the piece offers a concrete substitution technique — convert each negative thought into a command for future action, with three worked examples supplied. The author's framing is that the best leaders refuse to let the inner critic seize the internal microphone. The closing insists the negative commentary is a habit that must be actively fought, with command-substitution deployed every time the critic surfaces.
points: The piece's actionable core is the substitution drill: replace each negative thought with a command for a specific future action rather than trying to argue with it.
The author takes a position on causality — poor thoughts lead to poor performance rather than the other way round — which is what makes self-talk worth managing at all.
Inner commentary is accepted as natural and stress-relieving, so the target is the quality of the narration, not its existence.
The memorable image is the inner critic grabbing the internal microphone, with the leader's job being to keep it out of his hands.
Negative self-talk is framed as a habit that hardens with repetition, making early interruption more important than occasional correction.
quotes: The ongoing commentary is both natural and a way to relieve stress. But the quality of the narration matters. Leaders who become nasty inner critics undermine their ability to perform.
Does poor performance lead to poor thoughts or do poor thoughts lead to poor performance? The smart money is on the latter. The way you talk to yourself is a reflection of your focus.
Once you’re used to your own trash talk, the confidence required to perform at your best is exceedingly hard to muster. Who you are on the inside is reflected by how you perform on the outside.

The mind guides action and the science points to the fact that positive self-talk improves performance. The internal dialogue you have with your inner voice either promotes or takes away confidence. The best leaders work hard not to allow the inner critic to grab ahold of the internal microphone.
Don’t let your self-talk turn to the dark side. Fight off the negative commentary that can quickly become a habit. Substitute a command for action anytime the critic pops up in your head.
Never let the inner curmudgeon prevail. Your performance depends on it.
